items.question_en: The y-component of vector A⃗ is +3.0 m if A⃗ makes an angle of 30° counter clockwise from the positive y - axis, the magnitude of A⃗ is (assume A⃗ is in x - y plane)

solution.approach: The y-component of a vector equals its magnitude times the cosine of the angle the vector makes with the y-axis.

steps.text: Write the y-component in terms of the magnitude and the angle measured from the y-axis.
Substitute the given y-component and solve for the magnitude.
Evaluate the magnitude.

common_mistakes.text: Using sin30° instead of cos30°, treating the given 3.0 m as if it were measured from the x-axis instead of the y-axis, gives 6 m.

concept_tags: resolving a vector along an axis

items.question_en: Find the component of vector P⃗ = 2î + 3ĵ along the direction of vector Q⃗ = î + ĵ.

solution.approach: The component of one vector along another equals their dot product divided by the magnitude of the second vector.

steps.text: Compute the dot product of P and Q.
Compute the magnitude of Q.
Divide the dot product by the magnitude of Q to get the component.

common_mistakes.text: Taking only the x-components, 2×1 = 2, and ignoring the y-components and the division by |Q⃗|, gives 2.
Inverting the formula and computing |Q⃗|/(P⃗·Q⃗) instead of (P⃗·Q⃗)/|Q⃗| gives √2/5.

concept_tags: component of a vector along another vector

items.question_en: Find the angle between the two vectors: a⃗ = 3i + 2j + 5k, b⃗ = 5i + 3j + k

solution.approach: The cosine of the angle between two vectors equals their dot product divided by the product of their magnitudes.

steps.text: Compute the dot product of the two vectors.
Compute the magnitude of each vector.
Divide the dot product by the product of the magnitudes and take the inverse cosine.

common_mistakes.text: Computing the ratio 26/√1330 correctly but applying the inverse tangent instead of the inverse cosine confuses the dot-product angle formula with the tangent formula.
Applying the inverse sine instead of the inverse cosine to the same correctly computed ratio also confuses which formula the dot product gives.

items.question_en: A projectile is thrown at a speed which is twice its speed at its maximum height. If R and H are its range and maximum height respectively then the ratio R/H is:

solution.approach: The speed at the top of the path is the horizontal component of the launch speed, so the given condition fixes the angle of projection.

steps.text: Set the launch speed equal to twice the speed at maximum height, which is the horizontal component u cosθ.
Write the ratio R/H using R = u²sin2θ/g and H = u²sin²θ/(2g).
Substitute θ = 60°.

common_mistakes.text: Forgetting to square sinθ in the maximum-height formula, using H = u²sinθ/(2g) instead of u²sin²θ/(2g), gives R/H = 4cosθ = 2.

items.question_en: A river has a steady speed of 'v'. A man swims upstream at a distance of 'd' and swims back to the starting point in total time 't'. The man can swim at a speed of '2v' in still water. If the time taken by the man in still water is 't₀' to complete the same length of swim, then t/t₀ is

solution.approach: Find the effective upstream and downstream speeds, add the two travel times, and compare with the still-water time for the same total distance.

steps.text: Write the effective speeds against and with the current, using the still-water speed 2v and current speed v.
steps.equation: upstream speed = 2v − v = v; downstream speed = 2v + v = 3v

steps.text: Add the times for the upstream and downstream legs, each of length d.
Find the still-water time for the same total distance, 2d, swum at speed 2v.
Divide the two times.

common_mistakes.text: Treating the round trip as covering the total distance 2d at a single combined speed v + 3v, giving t = 2d/4v and a ratio of 1/2 instead of 4/3.
Forgetting the still-water comparison also covers the distance d twice and using d alone instead of 2d gives a ratio of 8/3, matching no printed choice.

items.question_en: A projectile is given an initial velocity of (3i + 4j) m/s where, î is along the ground and ĵ is along the vertical. Assuming g = 10 m/s², if the equation of its trajectory can be written as (1/9)[βx + γx²], then the value of γ is

solution.approach: Write the standard trajectory equation from the given velocity components, then match its coefficients to the given form to read off γ.

steps.text: Write the trajectory equation using the given velocity components and g = 10 m/s².
Rewrite the expression with a common factor of 1/9, matching the given form.
Compare with y = (1/9)(βx + γx²) to read off γ.

common_mistakes.text: Forgetting to divide by 2 in the term gx²/(2v_x²) doubles that coefficient, giving γ = −10, which does not match any of the printed choices.

items.question_en: An ant starts from the origin and crawls 10 cm along the x − axis and then 20 cm along the y − axis. The dot product of the ant's displacement vector with the position vector of a point that makes 45° with the x − axis and has a magnitude of √2 cm is

solution.approach: Write the ant's displacement vector after its two straight-line legs, form the given position vector from its magnitude and angle, then take their dot product.

steps.text: The ant's displacement from the origin is fixed by the two legs it crawled.
Write the second vector from its given magnitude √2 cm and its 45° angle with the x-axis.
Take the dot product of the two vectors.

common_mistakes.text: Multiplying the finished dot product by the magnitude √2 a second time, after already using it to build the position vector, gives 30√2.
Dividing the dot product by √2 instead, perhaps confusing this step with finding a unit vector, gives 30/√2.

items.question_en: A person walks in such a way that he covers equal distance in each step. The person takes 2 steps forward towards east, then takes a right turn and walks 4 steps towards south, then takes a right turn and walks 6 steps towards west and then takes a right turn and walks further. The direction of his final position after a total of 20 steps walk with respect to his initial position is

solution.approach: Add up the east-west steps and the north-south steps separately to get the net displacement, then read off its direction.

steps.text: List the four legs of the walk and the number of steps in each, given a total of 20 steps and a right turn after every leg.
Combine the east-west steps into one number and the north-south steps into another.
steps.equation: East − West = 4 − 6 = −4 (net 4 west); North − South = 8 − 4 = 4 (net 4 north)

steps.text: Since the net westward and northward steps are equal, the final position lies exactly on the diagonal between west and north.

common_mistakes.text: Stopping the count after the third leg (12 steps: 2 east, 4 south, 6 west) gives an equal 4-west, 4-south displacement, a south-west direction not among the printed choices.

items.question_en: A bomb is dropped on an enemy post on the ground by an aeroplane flying horizontally with a velocity of 60 kmh⁻¹ at a height of 490 m. At the time of dropping the bomb, the horizontal distance of the aeroplane from the enemy post so that the bomb hits the target is

solution.approach: Convert the plane's speed to metres per second, find the time to fall 490 m under gravity, and multiply to get the horizontal distance.

steps.text: Convert the plane's speed from kilometres per hour to metres per second.
Find the time for the bomb to fall 490 m, taking g = 9.8 ms⁻².
Multiply the plane's speed by this time to get the horizontal distance the bomb must be released before the target.

common_mistakes.text: Using g = 10 ms⁻² instead of 9.8 ms⁻² gives a fall time of 7√2 s and a horizontal distance near 165 m, close to but not matching any printed choice exactly.

items.question_en: The angular speed of a particle moving in a circular path is doubled. Then, the centripetal acceleration of the particle is

solution.approach: Centripetal acceleration is proportional to the square of the angular speed at a fixed radius, so doubling the angular speed multiplies it by four.

steps.text: Write the centripetal acceleration in terms of angular speed and radius.
Double the angular speed while the radius stays fixed.
Compare the new value with the original.

common_mistakes.text: Treating the centripetal acceleration as directly (not quadratically) proportional to the angular speed leads a student to conclude it merely doubles.

items.question_en: A cannon placed on a cliff at a height of 375 m fires a cannon ball with a velocity of 100 ms⁻¹ at an angle of 30° above the horizontal. The horizontal distance between the cannon and the target is (Acceleration due to gravity = 10 ms⁻²)

solution.approach: Resolve the initial velocity, use the vertical motion to find the time to reach the ground below the cliff, then multiply by the horizontal speed.

steps.text: Resolve the velocity into horizontal and vertical components.
Write the vertical displacement equation, taking the net drop to the ground as 375 m below the firing point.
Rearrange into a standard quadratic and solve for the positive time.
Multiply the horizontal speed by the time of flight to get the horizontal distance.

common_mistakes.text: Ignoring the initial upward vertical velocity and treating the fall as starting from rest at the cliff top gives a flight time of 5√3 s, which multiplies by 50√3 to give exactly 750 m.

items.question_en: A body P is projected at an angle of 30° with the horizontal and another body Q is projected at angle of 30° with the vertical. If the ratio of the horizontal ranges of the bodies P and Q is 1:2, then the ratio of the maximum heights reached by the bodies P and Q is

solution.approach: Write the angle body Q makes with the horizontal, then use the given range ratio together with the range and height formulas to find the height ratio.

steps.text: Body Q's angle with the vertical is 30°, so its angle with the horizontal is 90° − 30° = 60°.
Write the range ratio using R = u²sin2θ/g, noting sin2θ_P and sin2θ_Q are equal.
Write the maximum height ratio using H = u²sin²θ/(2g) and substitute the speed ratio found above.

common_mistakes.text: Misreading Q's 30° as already measured from the horizontal (not converting it to 60°) gives a height ratio of 1:2, which is not among the printed choices.

items.question_en: From a height of 'h' above the ground, a ball is projected up at an angle 30° with the horizontal. If the ball strikes the ground with a speed of 1.25 times its initial speed of 40 ms⁻¹, the value of 'h' is (acceleration due to gravity = 10 ms⁻²)

solution.approach: Use conservation of energy between the launch point and the ground, since gravity does no work on the horizontal motion, to relate the speeds to the height.

steps.text: Write the final speed in terms of the initial speed.
Apply energy conservation between the launch point, at height h above the ground, and the ground.
Substitute the known values and solve for h.

common_mistakes.text: Using only the vertical component of the initial velocity, 40sin30° = 20 m/s, instead of the full launch speed 40 m/s gives h = 105 m, not among the printed choices.

items.question_en: A ball projected at an angle of 45° with the horizontal crosses two points at equal heights separated by a distance at times 2 s and 8 s respectively. The horizontal distance between the two points is (Acceleration due to gravity = 10 ms⁻²)

solution.approach: Two points at equal height on a projectile's path are reached at times symmetric about the time of maximum height, which fixes the initial speed.

steps.text: The two times of equal height are symmetric about the time to reach maximum height.
Use the time to maximum height to find the initial speed, with the projection angle 45°.
steps.equation: t_top = u sin45°/g → 5 = u sin45°/10 → u = 50√2 m/s

steps.text: Find the horizontal component of the velocity, which stays constant through the flight.
Multiply the horizontal speed by the time between the two points to get the horizontal distance.

common_mistakes.text: Using the full time of flight, 10 s (twice t_top), instead of the 6 s gap between the two given points gives 500 m.

items.question_en: The vertical displacement (y in metre) of a projectile in terms of its horizontal displacement (x in metre) is given by y = (√3x − 0.2x²). The time of flight of the projectile is (Acceleration due to gravity = 10 ms⁻²)

solution.approach: Compare the given trajectory equation with the standard form to find the angle of projection and the initial speed, then compute the time of flight.

steps.text: Compare the coefficient of x with tanθ from the standard trajectory equation.
Compare the coefficient of x² with g/(2u²cos²θ) to find the initial speed.
Compute the time of flight using T = 2u sinθ/g.

common_mistakes.text: Forgetting to take the square root after solving u² = 100 and carrying u = 100 into the time-of-flight formula gives 10√3 s, not any of the printed choices.
